To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the magnetism of the 3d transition metal oxides can be understood by using the concept of the localized electron; (b) the magnetism is due to an electron-electron exchange interaction; and (c) the exchange interaction is due to a quantum mechanical effect.

the magnetism of the transition metals is a quantum phenomenon that depends on the occupation of the magnetic d states, that the magnetic susceptibility is determined by the number of unpaired d electrons, and that the magnetic moment is given by the spin of these d electrons, i.e. by the number of d holes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the application of quantum mechanics to the study of the magnetic properties of solids.
the development and application of new theoretical methods to the solution of fundamental problems in magnetism.
the development of a quantum theory of magnetism.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the quantum theory of magnetism is still in its infancy.

the quantum theory of magnetism is still incomplete and that the most pressing problems are the understanding of the magnetic properties of transition elements and of the magnetic interactions in the transition elements.

quantum mechanics has provided the theoretical foundation for the understanding of magnetism, and that the quantum mechanical approach has been successful to a degree that is almost without parallel in other fields of physics.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have been able to show that a large number of the most interesting and puzzling properties of the magnetic susceptibility can be explained by the theory of electron correlation.

we have shown that the quantum theory of magnetism, as it is understood today, is a very powerful tool for understanding and predicting the behavior of magnetic materials, and that the quantum theory is the only one which is capable of accounting for the observed facts.

the theory of magnetism has been developed to such a degree in recent years that we are in a position to understand the magnetic properties of all substances, both ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, ferrimagnetic, and paramagnetic.

the magnetic moment of the ground state of the hydrogen atom is not zero, but it has a finite value, which is 0.001 Bohr magnetons.
